lines: Lecture six goes through the imaging techniques.
No technique is perfect. The safe ones often lack resolution or sensitivity, and the deep or sharp ones use radiation.
So for each technique, ask three questions. How does it work? Is it invasive? And how do nanoparticles improve it?
MRI works on the hydrogen protons in the water of our tissues. Each proton spins like a tiny magnet, normally pointing in random directions.
The strong magnetic field of the scanner lines them up.
A radio-frequency pulse then pushes them out of line.
When the pulse is switched off, the protons realign, and they release energy.
A coil detects that energy. Different tissues release different amounts.
A computer turns it into an image. No ionizing radiation is used, so MRI is non-invasive.
MRI has relatively low sensitivity, so it uses contrast agents.
The common one, gadolinium, has two problems. It is toxic, and it spreads everywhere in the body.
Nanoparticles help in two ways. First, magnetic nanoparticles, such as superparamagnetic iron oxide, S P I O, can themselves be biocompatible contrast agents.
Second, a nanoparticle can carry the existing agent. Encapsulate it, stabilize it, coat it with a biocompatible polymer, and target it. That decreases toxicity and side effects.
And one important parameter: after any modification, the magnetic properties must be kept. He said he may ask these two points.
PET and SPECT both use radioactive tracers and gamma rays. So both are invasive, and both are expensive.
In PET, the tracer, for example fluorine eighteen, emits a positron.
The positron meets an electron. They annihilate, and two gamma rays of five hundred eleven kilo electron volts fly out in opposite directions.
In SPECT, the tracer, technetium ninety-nine m, emits a gamma ray of one hundred forty-one kilo electron volts directly. No positron, no electron.
The nanoparticle's role: carry the radiotracer to the target, so gamma rays are not produced all over the body.
Photoacoustic imaging: photo means light, acoustic means sound. He said you should completely describe its three steps.
Step one. A laser pulse illuminates the tissue.
Step two. The absorbed light excites electrons. They relax back to the ground state and release the energy as heat.
Step three. The heated area expands abruptly, and this thermal expansion sends out a thermoacoustic wave.
An ultrasound transducer detects the wave. Light in, sound out.
It gives anatomical, functional and molecular contrast in one modality, several centimeters deep. Its contrast agents are plasmonic nanoparticles: gold, silver, and single-walled carbon nanotubes.
Ultrasound uses only sound. A probe sends high-frequency sound and listens for the echo, so it is non-invasive.
But the further the sound travels, the weaker the echo. Deep tissues are hard to image.
Its contrast agents are micro and nano bubbles: a gas core inside a shell. They stay inside the blood vessels.
Hit by ultrasound, the bubbles oscillate. They expand and contract without bursting, and give a strong nonlinear echo that improves the signal-to-noise ratio. He said he may ask this.
The shells evolved from no shell, which burst easily, to protein, lipid, polymer and hybrid shells.
Since no technique is perfect, multimodal imaging combines two in one hybrid scan, such as SPECT with CT, or PET with CT.
CT shows the anatomy: what the structures look like.
SPECT shows the function: blood flow to the heart, or bone affected by cancer.
Together, with nanomaterial contrast agents, they give the best diagnosis.
